In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of monoclonal antibodies as immunogens.
the use of anti-Id as a vaccine to circumvent the H-2-linked immunological restriction pattern observed in the response to HBsAg.
the regulation of the immune response by the major histocompatibility locus in mice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the immune response to anti-Id is regulated by immune response genes, as is the response to HBsAg.
the immune response to HBsAg in the H-2f strain is regulated by immune response genes linked to the H-2 locus.
anti-Id immunization can circumvent H-2-linked restriction and can elicit a T cell response in vivo in mice of the f haplotype.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the immune response to HBsAg is regulated by H- 2-linked immune response (Ir) genes and that anti-Id could circumvent these Ir gene restrictions.
the anti-Id is a useful tool for the study of the immune response to HBsAg.
the immune response to HBsAg is not regulated by H- 2-linked genes in the H-2f mouse strain, but is regulated in the H- 2d mouse strain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immune response to anti-Id can be regulated by H-1 linked immune response genes.
the immune response to HBsAg is controlled by immune response genes and that the immune response is not restricted by H-2 haplotypes when the immune response is primed with anti-Id.
the immune response to anti-Id can be used to elicit HBsAgspecific antibodies in mice of several haplotypes and in wild mice.
